title: UK and US crochet terminology
subtitle: Why the same word means different stitches in UK and US patterns, and how to convert
excerpt: A UK double crochet and a US double crochet are not the same stitch. Every stitch name shifts by one when you cross the Atlantic. This guide shows each equivalent.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A short stitch worked by inserting the hook, drawing up a loop, then pulling through both loops on the hook. Called single crochet in US patterns.
A tall stitch made with one yarn-over before insertion. Called double crochet in US patterns.

content.text: UK and US crochet patterns use the same words to describe different stitches. A UK
double crochet
is the same stitch as a US single crochet. A UK
treble

is the same stitch as a US double crochet. The UK system has no 'single crochet'; the US system has no 'treble' at the same height as the UK treble. Every stitch name shifts by one when you cross between the two conventions. Work out which convention a pattern uses before starting, or every row will produce the wrong stitch.
How to tell which convention a pattern uses
UK patterns use 'dc' for a short stitch with no yarn-over before insertion. US patterns use 'sc' for the same stitch.
If a pattern uses 'sc', it is US terminology.
If a pattern has no 'sc' but uses 'dc', it is likely UK terminology.
Most patterns state the convention explicitly at the top. Check there first.
Full conversion table
UK slip stitch (sl st) = US slip stitch (sl st). These are the same in both systems.
UK double crochet (dc) = US single crochet (sc)
UK half treble (htr) = US half double crochet (hdc)
UK treble (tr) = US double crochet (dc)
UK double treble (dtr) = US treble (tr)
UK triple treble (trtr) = US double treble (dtr)
Converting a US pattern to UK terminology
Confirm the pattern is US terminology by finding 'sc' in the abbreviations.
Write out the abbreviations list for the pattern with the UK equivalent next to each US abbreviation.
Read each row using your conversion note. Do not rely on memory mid-row.
Common problems

items.symptom: The finished piece is much taller than the pattern photo
items.cause: A US pattern was read with UK terminology. A US 'dc' (treble height) was substituted for a US 'dc' (double crochet height), making every stitch much taller than intended.
items.fix: Check whether the pattern is US or UK. If it is US, re-read with the conversion table applied.

items.symptom: A pattern says 'sc' but nothing in the abbreviations list explains it
items.cause: The pattern assumes the reader knows US terminology and has not defined sc.
items.fix: 'sc' is US single crochet, which is UK double crochet. Treat every 'sc' as 'dc' throughout.

content.text: What to try next

Take a US pattern you want to make and annotate the abbreviations section with UK equivalents before starting. Doing this once for a specific pattern is faster than re-checking the conversion table mid-row.
